candidate.blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation — alterations in body systems / impaired ventilation and airway management
candidate.educational_objective: Use individualized positioning and airway-support measures to reduce aspiration or obstruction risk in a drowsy postanesthesia client.

options.A: Keep the client flat and supine regardless of secretions so that positioning does not influence the airway
options.B: Position the client laterally or turn the head to the side as clinically appropriate and keep suction available while continuing respiratory assessment
options.C: Place the client prone because prone positioning is required after general anesthesia
options.D: Sit the client fully upright immediately even if the client's level of consciousness does not allow safe maintenance of that position

candidate.rationale: In a markedly drowsy client without a positioning contraindication, lateral or head-turned positioning can help secretions drain away from the airway while the nurse continues close respiratory assessment and has suction available. Postanesthesia care remains individualized; no single position is appropriate for every surgical client.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Airway assessment and protection are immediate priorities during postanesthesia recovery; positioning must be adapted to the client's clinical and surgical context.
candidate.source_locator: Postoperative Nursing Care — Phase I/PACU: close monitoring of airway and recovery indicators takes precedence as clients emerge from anesthesia
candidate.source_organization: National Library of Medicine / NCBI Bookshelf
candidate.stem: A client arrives in the PACU after general anesthesia. The client is very drowsy, is breathing spontaneously, and has oral secretions. There is no surgical or spinal restriction that prevents repositioning. Which nursing action best supports airway protection while the client is not fully alert?
